list.listitem: Excisional biopsy provides useful diagnostic information and can be definitive treatment for some malignant and precancerous lesions.

Full dermal thickness excision was previously recommended as the gold standard for diagnosis of skin malignancy. However, shave excisions/biopsies can be the procedure of choice for most atypical lesions and do not significantly affect survival rates.

For nodular lesions elevated above the level of the surrounding skin and lesions on a convex surface, such as the nose or the pinnae of the ear, shave biopsies are most appropriate to plan definitive care.
Superficial shave biopsy remains contraindicated when melanoma is suspected as tumor thickness guides treatment and is the main predictor of death due to malignant melanoma.
Deep shave excision with narrow margins is appropriate for melanoma when feasible.
Consider referral based on size, proximity to sensitive structures, and cosmetic outcomes based on the skill set of provider.

Mohs surgery is indicated for suspected or proven malignant lesions with high-risk features. High-risk features take into account size, location, histologic subtype, recurrent/refractory lesions, and previous history of radiotherapy. These include basal cell carcinomas with high-risk positive margins, a lesion diameter of greater than 2 cm, and high-risk locations (eyelid, brow, nose, central face, upper lip, ear, genitalia, areola/nipple, or the hands/feet/ankle). Morpheaform, sclerosing, micronodular, and infiltrating subtypes as compared to superficial and nodular forms have a higher risk of relapse. Squamous cell carcinoma that is recurrent or found in a high risk location such as the anogenital area, lip, ear, on a scar, histologic subtypes (infiltrative or desmoplastic invasion), greater than 2 cm in diameter, 4mm in depth, or extending beyond the subcutaneous tissue. Sentinal lymph node biopsy may be required for larger lesions, especially those present on the head or neck.
Refer large lesions that may require a skin graft or flap.
A confirmed diagnosis of melanoma requires re-excision. See for guidelines. Referral may be needed based on size, location, skills of provider, and need for sentinal node biopsy.

section.heading: Nonsterile Skin Excision Prep Tray on a Mayo Stand (Use Nonsterile Drape):

list.listitem: Nonsterile/clean gloves, skin-marking pen as needed, 4 x 4 gauze, alcohol prep pad, povidone-iodine solution, or other skin-cleansing agent, 1 to 3 mL syringe with a 25 to 30 gauge needle for injection, 18 to 22 gauge for drawing from bottle, 1% or 2% lidocaine (most common) or other anesthetic agents with epinephrine (reduces bleeding), optional 8.4% sodium bicarbonate solution for buffering and reduced stinging with injection, No. 15 disposable scalpel or blade with re-usable handle or a flexible shave excision blade, hemostatic agent (aluminum chloride or electrocautery - Silver nitrate or Monsel’s solution can cause tattooing), Mayo or tissue scissors, mask, face shield or eye protection as indicated for personal protection, formalin or other specimen container, and white petrolatum ointment and adhesive bandage strip.

section.type: Sterile Tray for Procedure on Mayo Stand (Place Items on Sterile Drape Covering Stand):
section.heading: Sterile Tray for Procedure on Mayo Stand (Place Items on Sterile Drape Covering Stand):

list.listitem: See non sterile section regarding anesthesia which is usually done with clean technique prior to the procedure with 10 to 15 minutes allowed for the epinephrine to cause vasoconstriction. Sterile gloves, skin-marking pen as needed, gauze, fenestrated disposable drape, non-fenestrated disposable drape (optional), sterile tape to anchor the fenestrated drape if not self-adhesive drape (optional), 1 to 3 hemostats (mosquito clamps), No. 15 disposable scalpel or blade and re-usable handle, needle holder, Mayo or tissue scissors, iris scissors for cutting sutures, Adson or rat tooth forceps, 4 x 4 gauze, cotton-tipped applicators (optional), electrocautery available (optional), and adhesive strips (optional), dressing and suture materials.
Ask about medication allergies, history of bleeding difficulties, anticoagulation, or current infection.
Obtain informed consent and document.

Medically-indicated conventional anticoagulants (aspirin and warfarin), direct-acting oral anticoagulants (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, and edoxaban), and antithrombotics (eg, ticlopidine and clopidogrel) should not be stopped for minor skin excisions. The risk of thrombotic events in patients who have anticoagulation stopped perioperatively for dermatologic procedures (1 in 12,816 procedures) outweighs the minor benefit of preventing postoperative bleeding, estimated at 0.4% for simple excisions. In patients who are taking warfarin (Coumadin), international normalized ratio (INR) levels should be below 3.0. Meticulous attention to hemostasis, postoperative occlusive dressings, and appropriate close monitoring of INR levels in patients taking warfarin, and use of electrocautery in superficial biopsies/excisions will mitigate bleeding complications.

Prior to injecting anesthesia, which may distort the skin and make vascular lesions less visible, consider using a skin-marking pen to draw the desired margin around the lesion, with an ellipse that is 3 times as long as the diameter of the lesion plus the desired the margin to prevent dog-ears at the corners. The corner angles are 30°. Align the long axis of the fusiform shape parallel to skin tension lines for optimal cosmetic results. For a deep shave excision, draw the desired margin around the lesion, usually 1 mm for atypical nevi/possible melanoma.

Suspected basal or squamous cell carcinoma: Perform a partial, simple shave technique on a representative portion of the lesion. If biopsy confirms basal or squamous cell carcinoma not completely excised, excise the lesion using for recommended margins for excision.

Melanoma: Once a diagnosis of melanoma is made, a re-excision is recommended. It is therefore important to keep the initial biopsy small and only large enough to completely remove the lesion with a narrow margin approximately 1 mm. Remove the lesion with a deep shave technique, 1 mm around the visible lesion, and at least 1 mm in depth for small lesions, deeper for thicker lesions. If there is remaining pigmented tissue after the initial deep shave technique, a second deeper pass should be made. If the lesion is too large to remove with a deep shave technique, biopsy the possible melanoma with a 4 mm punch at the deepest/most suspicious portion of the lesion. Removing more than the necessary amount of tissue will increase the diameter of the subsequent re-excision necessitating a more complex repair or grafting. Full-thickness excision or large margins can also affect the lymphatic drainage from the site of the original lesion altering the ease or effectiveness of sentinel node biopsy. See Table 1 for re-excision margins based on pathology. Definitive treatment of thick melanomas should be done in consultation with a skin malignancy specialist, and wide margins should only be accomplished after an initial diagnostic biopsy.
Povidine-iodine, chlorhexidine, and alcohol wipes are traditionally used for skin cleansing, despite insufficient evidence that they prevent postoperative wound infections.

The risk of vasoconstrictor-induced ischemia or necrosis is based on antiquated preparations. Using epinephrine may reduce the need for tourniquets, reduces the total volume of anesthetic, reduces bleeding and provides better and longer pain control during procedures. Epinephrine is not required or indicated to achieve full anesthetic effect in digital blocks. Allow 10 to 15 minutes for the epinephrine to cause vasoconstriction before proceeding with the biopsy or excision.

Pain from local anesthesia injections can be reduced by using smaller-gauge needles (25-30 gauge), injecting slowly over 30 seconds, warming or buffering the solution with 8.4% sodium bicarbonate (previously 1 mL buffer per 10 mL anesthetic, current evidence shows 1 mL buffer to 3 mL lidocaine is even more effective at reducing injection pain), pinching the skin just before and during infiltration, or using topical anesthetics on intact skin and covering with an occlusive dressing 1 to 4 hours before the procedure. See for maximum anesthesia dosages.

If the patient is allergic to a local anesthetic, substitute the amide (eg, lidocaine, bupivacaine) with an ester (eg, procaine) or substitute with 1% diphenhydramine (Benadryl), created by adding 1 mL of diphenhydramine [50 mg/mL solution] to 4 mL sterile saline. Note that the duration of action of injected diphenhydramine may not be as long as the other agents.

Topical anesthetics, such as lidocaine/prilocaine cream (eutectic mixture of local anesthetics), can be used in children and in patients who cannot tolerate injections. Apply the cream to intact skin and cover with an occlusive dressing 1 to 4 hours before the procedure.
For sterile technique, drape the area with a sterile drape.

Superficial shave biopsy: Advance the blade of a No. 15 scalpel or flexible blade with easy slicing strokes that are parallel to the skin with the tip of the blade beyond the lesion similar to slicing a loaf of bread.

Deep/Excisional shave: Gently flex the flexible blade to the desired arc to excise along the drawn margins. Bevel the edge down at approximately a 30° angle for the first third of the excision, slicing back and forth with a pendulum like movement. Level off for the middle third of the excision and bevel up at a 30° angle for the final third of the excision. If there is remaining pigmentation at the base of the excision, draw a wider margin and repeat the saucerization or utilize an alternate excision technique. If using a No. 15 blade, consider creating a wheal to elevate the lesion to achieve a deep shave using a flat blade. Alternatively, a 25-gauge needle may be used to transfix and elevate the lesion slicing underneath it with the scalpel blade to achieve a deep shave.

Eliptical excision: Incise smoothly and continuously along the outline of the planned elliptical excision from each corner, fully through the dermis, holding the scalpel perpendicular to the skin. Use sharp dissection with short strokes to sever the subcutaneous attachments under the ellipse and remove the full-thickness skin excision.
Attain hemostasis by compression, cautery, or topical hemostatic agents, such as Aluminum chloride hexahydrate.
Monsel's solution and silver nitrate can cause tattooing and damage to the skin and are no longer preferred for skin hemostasis.
Eliminate dead space and accurately approximate tissue layers with minimal tension. Skin margins should be level or slightly everted.

Wound closure is generally not required after shave excisions. Use of a hemostatic agent, direct pressure, or electrocautery generally suffices unless the shave goes full-thickness through the dermis into the subcutaneous tissues.
Closure can be done with sutures, tissue adhesives, staples, or skin-closure tapes. Tissue adhesives and tapes should only be used when there is no remaining tension on skin edges.

When there is excessive tension, undermine both edges of the excised tissue to release tension for better cosmetic results. This can be done using blunt or sharp dissection, and undermining 2 to 3 cm will gain 1 cm in tissue relaxation.
Subcutaneous closure: For deeper wounds, potential "dead" space is eliminated by using interrupted stitches inverted and buried with absorbable sutures (eg, Vicryl, Dexon).
Use nonabsorbable sutures for the skin including nylon (Ethilon, Dermalon) and polypropylene (Prolene).

Simple interrupted dermal suture: The stitch is as wide as it is deep, with equal distance from the suture's point of entry to the wound margin and equal distance between each stitch. Sutures should not be less than 2 mm apart in cosmetically sensitive areas and can be farther apart in other areas. A simple running dermal suture can also be used. It provides slightly less control of the wound margins but is faster to place and works well if the wound has already been approximated with deep sutures.

Vertical mattress suture (far-far near-near): This provides good closure for fragile skin prone to excessive tension by promoting wound eversion in areas that tend to invert in the posterior neck or concave skin surfaces. Also used when skin tension is present or for areas of thicker skin, such as palms, soles, or back. It increases closure strength and distributes wound tension better. The empty space should be closed with a deep suture prior to this style being performed.

Intradermal running suture: This is used to close linear wounds without significant tension and yields good cosmetic results with less scarring. Start the suture through the skin beyond the apex of the defect and emerge at the apex in the dermis. After running the suture, enter the opposite apex and emerge distal to the apex through the skin.The ends of the suture can be taped to the skin or secured by slip knots under slight tension to preserve margin approximation. Disadvantages include decreased strength and little wound eversion. An alternate technique is to place a small suture as an anchor near the apex of the lesion, then suture from within the defect emerging at the apex in the dermis. At the opposite apex, tie the suture to the last loop. To bury the knot, drive the needle underneath the original knot and emerge 1 cm outside of the wound edge, pulling tightly, and cutting the suture flush with the skin.
See for recommended suture size for different anatomic locations.

Tissue adhesives are useful for closing wounds or lacerations that are not under any tension. For elliptical excisions, the skin needs to be re-approximated with deep sutures first before considering using a tissue adhesive, including anesthesia and surgical set up which negates most of the benefit of using tissue adhesive alone for simple lacerations.

Cochrane authors found that, compared with sutures, tissue adhesives are similar in patient and operator satisfaction, infection rates, and cost. While they appear to be equivalent in strength to healed tissue at 7 days and provide a faster healing time, Cochrane authors found higher rates of wound dehiscence with adhesives vs sutures. (Number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome was 43.) In addition, studies comparing adhesives to tape demonstrated no differences in outcomes except that surgeon assessment of cosmetic appearance was better for tape.
A water-resistant covering negates the need for topical petrolatum or antibiotics and wound dressing. Removal of adhesive is not required as it will spontaneously peel off in 5 to 10 days.

Tissue adhesives should not be used in patients at higher risk of poor healing, such as patients with diabetes or immunosuppression. They should also be avoided on mucosal surfaces and areas that maintain moisture, such as the groin or axillae.

Before applying tissue adhesive, ensure that the wound edges approximate without tension. Crush the inner glass ampule and invert applicator. Apply adhesive over an evenly approximated wound with gentle brushing motions. Keep the adhesive from entering the wound. Hold the wound edges together for at least 30 seconds before releasing. Excess adhesive can be wiped away with a dry gauze if done immediately. There is a 10-second "grace period" before the adhesive becomes too polymerized to wipe away. If the adhesive cannot be wiped away, apply antibiotic ointment or white petroleum for 30 minutes to loosen the polymer for removal. Apply at least 3 layers of adhesive.

Wounds can be dressed and supported by adhesive tapes or covered with an an adhesive bandage over petrolatum. Wounds can be allowed to get wet in the first 48 hours without increasing the incidence of infection.

Avoid topical antibiotics containing neomycin or bacitracin as their allergy rates are 11% and 8%, respectively. White petrolatum ointment is as effective as antibiotic ointment in promoting wound healing with a minimal risk for induction of allergy and an equally low infection rate as antibiotic ointment.

Infection: If purulence is present, remove enough sutures to promote drainage and allow to heal by secondary intention. Prescribe systemic antibiotic if cellulitis develops, infection is extensive or patient has risk factors such as diabetes or other chronic illnesses. Mupirocin cream or ointment is as effective as oral cephalexin for the treatment of minor secondary wound infections. Infections under tissue adhesive can be treated with oral antibiotics. Purulence from a true infection will generally push the adhesive away from the skin. If not, wipe away adhesive after applying antibiotic ointment or white petrolatum for 30 minutes.
Wound dehiscence: Commonly caused by sutures cutting through tissue from excessively tight sutures, wound infection, or inflammation.
Stitch abscess: Remove tightly tied or buried sutures.
Suture granulomas: Can occur around buried sutures. Remove sutures.
Sinus tracts: They are usually caused by infection around buried nonabsorbable braided sutures. Remove sutures.

Bleeding: Compression and/or use topical hemostatic agent as mentioned above. May also use cautery and ligate vessels, if indicated. Investigate potential causes of bleeding diathesis if difficult to control.

Scar hypertrophy or keloid: Treat and/or prevent with excision, intralesional verapamil, intralesional steroids, cryosurgery, or topical silicone. Intralesional verapamil, while less commercially available, has similar efficacy and fewer adverse reactions than intralesional steroids.
See for guidelines regarding suture removal.

Time off from work is usually not necessary, unless the excision is over a joint or other area that could lead to opening of the wound because of excessive or repetitive tension on sutures (eg, heavy manual labor).

CPT codes for excision of malignant lesions depend on size and location: 11600 to 11646.
